bib.title: Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning. Shaokun Zhang, Yi Dong, Jieyu Zhang, Jan Kautz, Bryan Catanzaro, Andrew Tao, Qingyun Wu, Zhiding Yu, Guilin Liu (NVIDIA, Penn State, UW). arXiv:2505.00024v2, 12 May 2025. Preprint, no venue stated.

COVERAGE: All 60,731 chars read (17 pages). Abstract, intro, related work, method, experiments (Tables 2-5, Figs 3-6), conclusion and appendices A-E (benchmarks, Table 6 hyperparameters, Fig 7 curves, examples, prompt) were read in full. The reference list (about chars 41,000-55,000) was skimmed for origins only. There is no limitations section.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Pure rule-based RL (GRPO) with a binary reward on format plus exact tool-call match trains tool-calling models with no reasoning-trace supervision. Tool-N1-7B/14B beat GPT-4o on BFCL overall.
  number: BFCL Overall: Tool-N1-14B 85.97, Tool-N1-7B 84.82, GPT-4o 83.97, Gemini-2.0-Flash 82.94, ToolACE-8B 82.57, Hammer2.1-7B 81.88, xLAM-2-70b 80.70, Qwen2.5-7B-Inst 76.95.
  setup: Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct backbones, BFCL v3 Live and Non-Live single-turn only (multi-turn excluded), leaderboard snapshot 2025-04-13, official script.
  quote: "Tool-N1-7B 77.00 95.00 94.50 90.50 82.17 80.44 62.50 70.83 89.25 80.38 84.82" and "Tool-N1-14B 80.58 96.00 93.50 92.00 84.10 81.10 81.25 66.67 90.52 81.42 85.97" and "GPT-4o 79.42 95.50 94.00 83.50 84.88 79.77 87.50 75.00 88.10 79.83 83.97"
  where: Table 2, p.7
  Note: the text claims 7B beats GPT-4o "by 0.85%", which matches 84.82 minus 83.97. The margin is under 1 point, and Tool-N1-7B does not win every subcategory. It scores 62.50 on Live Parallel against GPT-4o's 87.50.
- Pure RL does at least as well as SFT-then-RL, so SFT-then-RL is not necessarily better for tool calling.
  number: Avg: 100% RL 83.24, 50% SFT+50% RL 83.17, 100% Reason-SFT 82.71, 100% No-Reason SFT 81.47.
  setup: 5,518 ToolACE single-turn instances, reasoning traces distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and filtered for correct format and correct call. Qwen2.5-Instruct (size not stated in this table). Equal data budgets. The SFT+RL vs RL gap is 0.07 points, with one run each and no variance reported.
  quote: "we do not observe improved performance under equal data budgets in the tool-calling setting (83.17% vs. 83.24%). In fact, SFT may even hinder performance"
  where: Sec 5.3.2, Table 3, p.9
- Reasoning traces add little in SFT.
  number: No-Reason SFT 81.47 vs Reason-SFT 82.71 (100% data).
  quote: "No-Reason SFT performs only slightly worse than Reason-SFT (e.g., 81.47% vs. 82.71%), suggesting that providing reasoning traces during SFT offers limited additional benefit."
  where: p.9
- Binary reward beats fine-grained partial-credit reward, especially on Live, which the authors attribute to reduced reward hacking. This is their attribution and was not tested.
  number: Avg 84.82 (binary with reasoning format) vs 83.74 / 82.58 / 81.94 for the fine-grained variants. Live 80.38 vs 76.61.
  setup: Tool-N1-7B. Fine-grained reward gives 0.2 for correct reasoning format and a further 0.2 for matching function name. Binary gives 1.0 only if all parts are correct.
  quote: "Tool-N1 achieves consistently better performance with binary rewards, particularly on the Live subset (80.38% vs. 76.61%), which involves more realistic inputs. We attribute this to reduced reward hacking"
  where: Table 4, pp.10-11
- Removing the think-format constraint from the binary reward hurts. This ablation changes the reward's format requirement during training, not the prompt.
  number: Live 80.38 to 76.24; Avg 84.82 to 81.94.
  quote: "removing the reasoning format constraint significantly hurts performance (dropping from 80.38% to 76.24%)"
  where: p.11
- RL beats SFT on the same data sources.
  number: Tool-N1-7B trained on xLAM alone beats the xLAM-8B SFT model by 6.36%. Trained on the ToolACE subset alone it beats ToolACE-8B by 1.62%. Table 5 Avg: Raw Qwen 67.54, xLAM-8B 75.65, ToolACE-8B 82.57, Tool-N1 w/o ToolACE 82.01, w/o xLAM 83.63, full 84.82.
  quote: "outperforms the xLAM-8B SFT model by 6.36%, and the Tool-N1-7B model trained solely on the ToolACE subset exceeds the ToolACE-8B SFT model by 1.62%, despite using only a subset of the data"
  where: Sec 5.4.1, Table 5, p.11
  Caveat: the SFT baselines are 8B (Llama-based) models and Tool-N1 is Qwen 7B, so the backbone differs.
- On other benchmarks the 7B model gains a lot over its base and the 14B model beats GPT-4o.
  number: API-Bank accuracy: LLaMA-3.1-Base-8B 60.41, GPT-4o-mini 73.10, GPT-4o 77.16, Tool-N1-7B 81.28, Tool-N1-14B 82.19. ACEBench: 50.63 / 81.63 / 82.34 / 86.00 / 87.00 (the y-axis labels list GPT-4o after the Tool-N1 models, so the mapping of the last values to models is my reading of the plot, unverified).
  setup: Single-turn only, multi-turn cases excluded. API-Bank uses Call mode only.
  quote: "Tool-N1-7B achieves substantial absolute improvements of over 20% on APIBank and over 30% on ACEBench compared to the base models."
  where: Fig 3, p.7-8
  Caveat: the text says "Tool-N1-14B surpasses GPT-4o by 5.03%". In Fig 3a, 82.19 minus 77.16 is 5.03, so that figure refers to API-Bank. The intro says "approximately 2% and 5%" improvement over GPT-4o on BFCL and API-Bank.
- RL gains grow with model size and depend on backbone.
  number: Sizes 0.5B-14B Qwen2.5-Instruct, with post-training gains described as limited at 0.5B and 1.5B. Backbones: Qwen-2.5-7B Non-Live/Live 89.1/80.2 vs LLaMA-3.1-8B 88.1/76.2 vs LLaMA-3-8B 86.5/65.8 (the figure labels are ambiguous; this is read from the plot text).
  quote: "performance improvements from post-training are limited for smaller models (0.5B and 1.5B), whereas larger models exhibit substantial gains."
  where: Sec 5.3.1, Figs 4-5, pp.8-9
  Caveat: the Qwen advantage is attributed to Qwen's stronger reasoning (citing Gandhi et al., 2025) without a test.
- Response length did not grow during RL, unlike R1-style math training. The authors suggest long chains are not needed for tool calling.
  number: none (Fig 6b average length about 80-180 tokens).
  quote: "Figure 6b shows no significant increase in response length throughout training, which contrasts with trends observed in prior R1-style training works"
  where: Sec 5.4, p.10
- Data preparation and the training recipe.
  number: Table 1: xLAM 60,000 raw and 60,000 after processing, single-turn only. ToolACE single-turn 10,500 raw and 8,183 after processing. ToolACE multi-turn 800 raw and 1,470 after processing, because multi-turn trajectories are split into single-step instances.
  recipe: Verl, batch size 1024, lr 1e-6, temperature 0.7, entropy coefficient 0 ("introducing entropy negatively impacts exploration"), KL 1e-3, 7 epochs, 5 rollouts per prompt, max prompt 4096 and max response 8192 tokens, 4 nodes x 8 H100 80GB. The same hyperparameters are used for 7B and 14B.
  quote: "Training is performed with a batch size of 1024 and a learning rate of 1× 10−6. The temperature is fixed at 0.7. We set the entropy coefficient to 0"
  where: Sec 5.1, Table 6, pp.7, 16
- Reward definition. The reward is 1 only if both the output contains <think>...</think> and <tool_call>...</tool_call> and the parsed tool call matches the ground truth in name and all argument key-value pairs. The match is by dictionary, so argument order does not matter.
  number: none (binary 0/1)
  quote: "assigns a reward of 1 if both of the following conditions are met:(1) Format Correctness ... (2) Tool Call Correctness:The predicted tool call 𝑎𝑡∈ 𝑂𝑡 exactly matches the ground-truth call 𝑎*𝑡 in both tool name and all argument key-value pairs."
  where: Sec 4.3, Eq 5, p.6

LIMITS
- No limitations section. The authors concede nothing explicit beyond noting that SFT may hurt (citing Chen et al., 2025).
- Evaluation is single-turn only. Multi-turn is excluded from BFCL, API-Bank and ACEBench. Despite the title and the problem formulation (action-observation history), no multi-step agent loop, real tool execution or observation feedback is trained or evaluated.
- The SFT vs RL study uses one data set (5,518 ToolACE instances), one run per recipe, and no variance. Differences of 0.07 to 0.5 points are small.
- The reward is exact match against a single ground-truth call, so alternative valid calls can be penalized. This is not discussed.
- Causal explanations (reward hacking, Qwen's reasoning strength) are asserted, not tested.
- Dated: the BFCL snapshot is 2025-04-13 and the baselines are early-2025 models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0-Flash, DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3.1). Model-size scaling covers only Qwen2.5 up to 14B.
- Some text has typos ("Tool-N11", "vertain"), and the Fig 7 caption says "minimum response length" while the Fig 7c y-axis is unlabeled.

BUILDS ON
- DeepSeek-R1 and rule-based R1-style RL (Guo et al., 2025). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024, DeepSeekMath). Verl (Sheng et al., 2024, HybridFlow) for RL training. LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) for SFT.
- Data: xLAM (Zhang et al., 2024) with APIGen (Liu et al., 2024), and ToolACE (Liu et al., 2024).
- The SFT-vs-RL argument draws on Chen et al., 2025 (SFT or RL? an early investigation into R1-like vision-language models). Also Gandhi et al., 2025, and Pan et al., 2024 (reward hacking).
- Related RL-with-tools work: Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) and ReTool (Feng et al., 2025). The authors say these use a single general-purpose tool.
- Benchmarks: BFCL (Yan et al., 2024), API-Bank (Li et al., 2023), ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025).
- Baselines: ToolACE-8B, xLAM-2 (Prabhakar et al., 2025), Hammer2.1 (Lin et al., 2024).
- Prompted tool use: ReAct (cited as Yao et al., 2023). The authors say the lightweight template lets the model "be more easily integrated with more sophisticated prompting strategies (Yao et al., 2023)".

CODE (Appendix E, p.17 and Fig 2, p.5; the arguments format is garbled in the extraction)
"In each action step, you MUST:
1. Think about the reasoning process in the mind and enclosed your reasoning within <think></think> XML tags.
2. Then, provide a json object with function names and arguments within <tool_call> </tool_call> XML tags."
"3. Make sure both the reasoning and the tool call steps are included together in one single reply."
Reward (Eq 5): r = 1 if FormatCorrect(O) AND ToolCallMatch(a, a*), otherwise 0.
Appendix D example output: <think>To search for a hair stylist in Lafayette, Louisiana, I will use the "Services_1_FindProvider" function with the required city parameter.</think> <tool_call>[{"name": "Services_1_FindProvider", "arguments": {"city" "Lafayette, LA"}}]</tool_call> (the colon after "city" is missing in the extraction).

FIGURES (text only; I did not run the figures script, and the captions below come from the extraction)
- Fig 1, p.2: training pipeline. Query plus tool list go to the policy, which rolls out outputs. A rule-based reward gives 1 for correct format and call, otherwise 0. GRPO with a KL loss to a reference model. Shows the whole recipe at a glance.
- Fig 2, p.5: thinking template with <think> and <tool_call> tags.
- Fig 3, p.7: API-Bank and ACEBench bar charts.
- Fig 4, p.8: scaling 0.5B to 14B, RL vs raw.
- Fig 5, p.8: backbone comparison.
- Fig 6, p.10: KL, response length and validation curves.
- Fig 7, p.16: reward, entropy and min response length.
- Fig 8, p.17: full prompt.
